name: Celadon
lede: Celadon is a pale, grey-tinged green, named in seventeenth-century France for a shepherd in a novel and then attached to the grey-green glazed porcelain of China.

sections.title: A shepherd's name
sections.body:
Celadon is named for a fictional shepherd, not for China [1][2]. Honoré d'Urfé's pastoral romance *L'Astrée*, published between 1607 and 1627, runs to 60 books and some 5,400 pages, and follows Céladon, a lovelorn shepherd trying to win back his Astrée after a quarrel [1]. It was translated across Europe, adapted for the stage, and started a vogue for woodland-green clothes named for its hero [1]. Finlay describes the hero as wearing a pale green suit with swirling green ribbons, and says that all of Paris was soon dressed à la celadon [2].

Paterson, citing Partridge, agrees that the word comes from a rustic lover in French pastoral poetry [3]. Finlay mentions a rival story, in which the word recalls Saladin sending forty pieces of green ware to Sultan Nureddin in 1117, but he calls the novel the more interesting theory [2]. St Clair gives the novel flatly [1].

The color word then moved to the pottery. The Chinese had been making grey-green glazed wares for centuries before d'Urfé's hero existed [1]. European buyers, far down the trade routes, understood little of the classifications behind the ware, and the patterns and colors that told a trained eye its place and age meant nothing to them [1]. Finlay notes that Chinese porcelain became highly fashionable in seventeenth-century Europe, and that some of it happened to be this popular color [2].

sections.title: What the glaze is
sections.body:
Celadon is a family of glazes, not a single color. St Clair describes pieces that are usually greyish green but run from blues to greys and ochers and even blacks, and which owe their color to iron in the clay and to iron oxide, manganese oxide and quartz in the glaze [1]. They are fired at just under 2,100 degrees Fahrenheit, with the oxygen cut sharply halfway through [1]. Finlay puts the cause plainly: a small amount of iron, with more iron giving more green, and a typical celadon glaze holding about 2 per cent while anything over 6 per cent goes black [2].

The glaze itself comes from the mountains. Finlay explains that the kiln wood supplied the fuel and, as ash mixed with kaolin, the glaze, while the clay made the body, so a bowl comes entirely from the hillside [2].

The crackle is often deliberate. Many pieces carry a fine network of cracks, as fine as the veins of a leaf, placed on purpose to make the surface resemble [[gem:jade|jade]] [1]. Chinese buyers prize the dark lines on the pale green, and Rosemary Scott, the Christie's consultant, told Finlay that the bowl becomes perfect by being slightly imperfect [2]. She added that crackle glazes keep cracking for some time after firing, so that a piece may suddenly make a little ping in a quiet room [2].

sections.title: Mi se, the mysterious color
sections.body:
The most famous celadon was never seen by most of the people who wrote about it. Mi se, "mysterious color" or "secret color", was for a long time China's dearest and most exclusive pottery, kept for royal households, and hardly anyone outside the court had seen a piece [1]. Xu Yin, a tenth-century poet, imagined it as light carved from the moon to tint a mountain stream [1]. Scott points out that the Chinese word for secrecy can also mean reserved or held back, so the name may mean a ware kept for the court [2].

The proof came in 1987, when a secret chamber was found under the ruined pagoda of Famen temple, near Xi'an, after half of the brick tower had slid to the ground in a rainstorm in 1981 [2]. Finlay's account has the emperor's family donating a great treasure to Famen in 874, with the secret celadon among it, and a stone inventory in the chamber naming the pieces [2]. The inventory pushed the beginnings of mi se back by at least thirty years [2]. St Clair dates the rediscovery to the late 1980s [1].

The pieces were a disappointment to anyone expecting jade. St Clair calls the color a rather drab olive, and Finlay found the pieces brownish and plainish [1][2]. The ware comes from the Shanglinhu kilns in Zhejiang, and its glaze held about 3 per cent iron, against about 2 per cent in an ordinary celadon [2]. Finlay's reading of its appeal is that rulers surrounded by gold and silk may have prized something plain and earthy [2]. The Song court abandoned mi se, and the last reference to it is from 1068, in an encyclopedia of Song institutions [2].

sections.title: Celadon and the poison myth
sections.body:
A persistent claim is that celadon can detect or neutralize poison. It is a legend, and the books say where it came from [1][2]. The Ottoman rulers, who took Constantinople in 1453, collected hundreds of celadon pieces that can still be seen in the Topkapi Palace, and St Clair says they believed the ware was a natural antidote [1][2]. Finlay's source, the Islamic scholar Michael Rogers, calls the belief that the bowls were alexipharmic the likeliest reason for the collecting, but he does not know where the idea started and suspects it reached the Ottomans from Europe [2].

The test was tried. Jahangir, the Mughal emperor, is said to have had two condemned prisoners fed poisoned food, one on celadon and one on another dish, and both died [2]. The idea outlived the proof: Finlay found the same belief attached to the reddish-brown Gardner porcelain of nineteenth-century Russia, sold across Central Asia as a protector against poisoned food [2].

A different legend concerns a Song ware called Chai, said to be blue as the sky, bright as a mirror and thin as paper [2]. There are no known or even suspected examples, and some scholars suspect a hoax repeated from author to author [2]. Chai ware is a legend, a color that exists only in descriptions.

sections.title: Celadonite and green earth
sections.body:
The word has a second life in mineralogy. The mineral celadonite was named by Glocker in 1847 from the French *céladon*, meaning sea-green, for its usual color [4]. Paterson lists celadonite as another name for *terre verte*, the green earth pigment, and Pigment Compendium sends "celadon green" to its green earth entry [3][4].

So there are two celadons in the records. One is the pale glaze-green of porcelain. The other is the library's *Celadon Green* from Maerz and Paul (1930), a greyer, darker olive, #8E9775, with a first recorded date of about 1650 and a variant spelling, *Seladon Green*, dated 1705 [6]. Related names on our chart are [[celadon-green]], [[sage-green]], [[pistachio]] and [[sea-green]] [6].

sections.title: The swatch and the glaze
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is the pale gentle green of paint chips and color lists. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 puts the name in block 148, Wikipedia lists a slightly more saturated #ACE1AF and the xkcd survey a bright #BEFDB7 [6]. A real celadon bowl differs from all of these: St Clair and Finlay both stress that the glaze can be grey, olive or brown, and the secret mi se was a murky olive [1][2].

In Baty's tables of early color nomenclatures, *celadon-green* appears in several lists, in the slot where another list has celandine green [5]. The Japanese name for the ware's color, *seiji-iro* (青磁色), "celadon color", is on our library as a pale greyish sage, #819C8B [6]. To see more of it, tilt a celadon bowl against the light: patterns incised under the glaze show up in the thin green [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Celadon is a rare painted color but an easy one to spot. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 34 works [7]. It is a light color: in those paintings 82 per cent of it sits among the highlights and the rest in the mid-tones [7]. The decade with the highest share is the 1910s, where 6 of 523 paintings qualify, eight times the archive rate [7].

The painter who stands out is Van Gogh: 4 of his 49 paintings in the archive carry it, 57 times the archive rate [7]. The largest share is in his *Roses* of 1890, where it covers 44 per cent of the canvas, and *La Mousmé* of 1888 follows at 42 per cent [7]. [[painting:nga-72328|Roses]] is the painting whose pink flowers faded, a story told in the [[irresistible]] article [9]. The earliest example is Bartolomeo di Giovanni's *Stories of Saint Benedict* of 1488, at 27 per cent [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color and not a pigment test [7].

In Google Books *celadon* is already at about 58 per cent of its peak in 1800, peaks in 1808, and returns to 94 per cent of the peak in 1980 [8]. It is one of the few color words that never went out of use.
